 Explainer-What is Shamonda virus and what are the risks to humans and animals?
 Thursday, 22 Oct 2026
 | 10:50 PM MYT
 share 
 bookmark 
 Cows graze near the drought-stricken Doubs River near Montbenoit, France, August 18, 2026. REUTERS/Denis Balibouse 
 PARIS, Oct 22 (Reuters) - France has reported ⁠the first known human case of Shamonda virus in a patient who died, ⁠raising questions about the risks posed by a livestock virus that has reached Europe ‌this year decades after first being detected in Nigeria.
 WHAT IS SHAMONDA VIRUS?
 Shamonda is transmitted by biting midges and mainly affects cattle, though infections have also been identified in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas.
 It belongs to the same group ​as Schmallenberg virus, which causes reproductive disorders in livestock.
 WHERE HAS ⁠IT SPREAD?
 First detected in cattle in Nigeria ⁠in 1965, it has since been found in parts of Africa and Asia.
 First identified in ⁠Europe ‌in late July, by October 20 cases had been reported in more than a dozen European countries including in top cattle breeders France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.France said the ⁠virus had been likely been circulating in the country since ​the spring.
 HOW DANGEROUS IS IT ‌FOR ANIMALS?
 Symptoms include fever, diarrhoea and reduced milk production.
 More serious complications include abortions and ⁠severe foetal malformations. ​Neurological disorders have also been reported in some horses.
 The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) says the long-term impact of the European variants remains uncertain.
 WHAT IS THE RISK TO HUMANS?
 The first documented patient was being treated ⁠for a serious illness at a hospital in Lyon ​and had a severely weakened immune system.
 The UN's World Health Organization said that based on current information and knowledge of the transmission of closely related viruses, this was an isolated human case and ⁠unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time.
 French authorities suspect infection occurred through a midge bite in eastern France, where the virus circulated among livestock earlier this year.
 They said the patient's brain complications were very likely linked to Shamonda, although investigations into the infection and death are ​continuing. WHAT IS ITS CURRENT STATUS?Shamonda is not a disease listed ⁠by the WOAH and countries are therefore not required to notify WOAH of cases under its ​disease-specific reporting obligations.
 Nor is it listed under the European Union's ‌Animal Health Law framework, meaning it is not ​subject to EU disease-specific mandatory surveillance.
 Because of this, available data may not provide a complete picture of its spread.
 (Reporting by Sybille de La Hamaide; editing by Jason Neely)
